lesson.title: Slope Over a Stretch: The Average Rate of Change
lesson.summary: The average rate of change packages the rate-of-change idea into a single, computable number for any interval, by dividing the total change in output by the total change in input, exactly the way ordinary slope is computed between two points.
lesson.body:
Given a function f and an interval from x=a to x=b, the average rate of change over that interval is defined as [f(b) - f(a)] divided by (b - a). This is simply the change in output divided by the change in input, the same ratio used to compute slope between two points, applied here to any two points that happen to lie on the graph of f. It answers the question: on average, across this whole interval, how many units did y move for every one unit that x moved?

The word "average" is doing real work here. As the previous section showed with f(x) = x^2, the function's actual rate of change is not constant, it speeds up as x increases. The average rate of change over an interval smooths all of that internal variation into one representative number, the same way an average speed over a trip smooths out the moments of speeding up and slowing down into a single number for the whole drive.

Take f(x) = x^2 again, now over the interval from a=1 to b=4. Compute f(1) = 1 and f(4) = 16. The average rate of change is [16 - 1] divided by [4 - 1] = 15/3 = 5. This means that, averaged across the whole interval from x=1 to x=4, y increased by 5 units for every 1 unit increase in x, even though the function was not actually climbing at a steady rate of 5 the entire time; it was climbing more slowly than that near x=1 and more quickly than that near x=4.

A physical interpretation makes this concrete. Suppose a ball's height above the ground is given by s(t) = t^3 for t in seconds, over the interval from t=0 to t=2. Then s(0) = 0 and s(2) = 8, so the average rate of change is [8 - 0] divided by [2 - 0] = 8/2 = 4. If s(t) measured position, this 4 would represent the average velocity over those two seconds, in whatever distance units s(t) is measured in per second, even though the object's actual instantaneous velocity was different at every moment along the way.

A subtler example shows why "average" can be misleading if taken too literally. Let f(x) = x^2 - 4x, and compute the average rate of change from x=0 to x=4: f(0) = 0 and f(4) = 16 - 16 = 0, so the average rate of change is (0 - 0)/(4 - 0) = 0/4 = 0. This might suggest the function never moves over that interval, but f(2) = 4 - 8 = -4, so the function actually dips down to -4 at the midpoint before climbing back up to 0. The average rate of change only reports the net effect between the two endpoints; it says nothing about the dip in between, which is exactly why a single average number can never fully substitute for knowing the rate of change at every point along the way.

Geometrically, the average rate of change over [a, b] is exactly the slope of the straight line connecting the two points (a, f(a)) and (b, f(b)) on the graph of f, a line called the secant line, which is examined closely later. Algebraically, the expression [f(b) - f(a)] divided by (b - a) is also the starting point for the difference quotient, and letting the interval shrink toward a single point is what eventually produces the instantaneous rate of change discussed next.
